paras: The Lower Merion manhunt for Elias Williams was a search by an armed citizens' posse in Lower Merion township, Pennsylvania, on 29 July 1903 for a Black man thought to be Williams, who was accused of killing Percy White. Residents had shot at the man two days earlier without hitting him, and the local police chief concluded that he was an escaped convict, "Cracker" Crummity, not Williams. Williams himself was arrested in Maryland on 31 July, amid reports that threats to lynch him were frequent.

Percy White was shot on 19 June 1903 in a field of his father's farm in Springfield township, Delaware County, near Swarthmore, and Elias Williams, a Black farmhand, was charged with the killing. Within days "bands of indignant citizens" and county authorities were searching the country between Media, Chester and Philadelphia, and a $500 reward was offered.

According to a Philadelphia dispatch dated 28 July, on the previous day people in Lower Merion "fearful for the safety of the women in the neighborhood" had chased a suspicious man and fired several shots at him before he escaped. On 28 July police were told that a man resembling Williams had been seen near the residence of the iron master Percival Roberts, and Chief Brookmyre searched the area. The chief returned to Ardmore convinced that the man was "Cracker" Crummity, alias Williams, a fugitive wanted in Savannah who had escaped from Moyamensing prison about two weeks before.

A dispatch of 29 July nonetheless described the quarry as "the colored man supposed to be Elias Williams" and said many residents of the suburb had spent the night tracking him. Volunteers armed with pitchforks and clubs and carrying lanterns answered a morning call, twenty-five of them by 8 o'clock, alongside mounted men. John Murphy, described as a citizen, took charge with the help of a private detective named Metlinger; no report of the search's outcome appears in the coverage.

On 31 July Baltimore detectives Hogan and Dick arrested Elias Williams on a farm near Cockeysville, Baltimore County, Maryland. A Maryland weekly wrote that the county had been thrown into "a great state of excitement" and that threats of lynching him if caught "were frequent." When he was taken from Baltimore to Media on 7 August, the hour was kept secret for fear that an attempt might be made to lynch him.

At his trial in Media in October, Williams testified that he fired only when White came toward him in a threatening manner, and the jury convicted him of second-degree murder after three hours. Judge Johnson sentenced him to twenty years in the Eastern Penitentiary, and a Baltimore County paper reported a $500 fine as well. Because the sheriff learned that White's friends resented the verdict, Williams was quietly sent to prison so that "trouble might be avoided."

The Lower Merion search reached print on 29 July in two white dailies far from the scene, the Evening Journal of Delaware and the Savannah Morning News. The Evening Journal headlined it "New Posse for Colored Man" over "Suspected Negro Murderer," called Williams "the alleged murderer" and said the suburb had been "terrorized," without mentioning doubts about the man's identity. The Savannah paper built its story around a local fugitive, the "Notorious Savannah Desperado," called Williams flatly "the murderer of Percy White," and presented the shooting as a response to fear for women.

Williams's arrest, transfer and trial ran more widely in white papers from Delaware to Utah, which often called him "the negro murderer" or "confessed murderer" before trial. The only Black-press item found, the Richmond Planet's 10 October report of the conviction under "Elias Williams Convicted," included his self-defense testimony but did not mention the Lower Merion posse or the lynching threats.

Reports disagree on who the hunted man was: the 29 July dispatch called him the man "supposed to be Elias Williams," but Lower Merion's police chief, after his own search, believed he was Crummity, and Williams's reported confession placed him in Maryland since the shooting. The papers also differed on White's home: the Evening Journal called him "the young Chester county farmer," while other reports placed his father's farm in Springfield township, Delaware County.

accounts.label: Lower Merion police chief
accounts.gist: After searching near the Roberts residence, Chief Brookmyre concluded the man was not Williams but the escaped Savannah convict 'Cracker' Crummity; residents had chased and shot at him the previous day.

accounts.label: Williams's reported confession
accounts.gist: Williams said he fled to Baltimore by train the night of the shooting and stayed there and then on a farm near Cockeysville.

accounts.label: Defense at trial
accounts.gist: Williams testified he fired only when White approached him threateningly after a warning, pleading self-defense.

framing.detail: Evening Journal headlined 'New Posse for Colored Man' and 'Suspected Negro Murderer', called Williams 'the alleged murderer' and the suburb 'terrorized', reporting the armed hunt without criticism.
Savannah Morning News headlined '"Cracker Crummity" Located in Philadelphia', called Williams 'the murderer of Percy White' and presented the shots fired as prompted by fear for women.
Arrest and trial wires called Williams 'the negro murderer' and 'confessed murderer' and noted fears of lynching.
Richmond Planet ran the Media conviction wire under 'Elias Williams Convicted', including the self-defense testimony, with no comment.
